sections.title: What is the Big Five?
sections.lead: A research-based taxonomy of broad personality traits, commonly remembered by the acronym OCEAN.

blocks.text: The Big Five began as an effort to organise the many words people use to describe personality. Researchers proposed that socially important differences become represented in language, then used factor-analytic methods to identify clusters among trait descriptions. Across multiple approaches, five broad families repeatedly appeared. Goldberg's work helped establish the 'Big Five' label and factor structure; later reviews integrated the model with questionnaire research and personality theory (Goldberg, 1990; McCrae & John, 1992; John & Srivastava, 1999).

The framework is mainly descriptive: it summarises regularities in thought, feeling and behaviour. It does not, by itself, explain every cause of personality, every motivation or every individual difference. Narrower facets, values, interests, abilities, identity, culture and life circumstances still matter.

blocks.alt: The five OCEAN continua: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness and Emotional Reactivity

sections.title: How personality assessment works
sections.lead: A valid interpretation depends on clear constructs, good items, transparent scoring and evidence from real users.

blocks.text: A student is not simply 'open' or 'not open', 'extrovert' or 'introvert'. Each domain represents a degree of typical expression. Middle scores can reflect genuine flexibility, context dependence or a mix of narrower tendencies. Extreme scores can be useful in some environments and costly in others.

items.q: Is the Big Five a personality type test?

a.text: No. It gives five continuous scores. Career Garage should not turn the scores into rigid types.

items.q: Is a high score always better?

a.text: No. Every level can support strengths and create trade-offs depending on the situation.

items.q: Is lower Extraversion the same as poor communication?

a.text: No. It may reflect a preference for lower stimulation or more preparation. Communication is a skill that can be developed.

items.q: Does high Emotional Reactivity mean a mental-health disorder?

a.text: No. The score reflects self-reported stress sensitivity in this item set and is not diagnostic.

items.q: Can personality change?

a.text: Traits show meaningful stability, but average levels and individual patterns can change with development, roles, experience and intervention.

items.q: Can the assessment choose a career for a student?

a.text: No. It can identify environment questions and development areas. Career decisions require multiple assessments and real evidence.

items.q: Why are some items opposite in meaning?

a.text: They help reduce automatic agreement and provide a basic response-quality check. They are reverse-scored.

items.q: Why use 60 questions?

a.text: Twelve items per domain provide enough breadth for development-stage testing while keeping completion practical. Quality matters more than adding more items.

items.q: Should all 13 Career Garage assessments be taken together?

a.text: No. Use separate sessions or a carefully designed combined pathway to prevent fatigue.

items.q: Can teachers see raw answers?

a.text: Only if the published privacy, consent and role-access model authorises it. Default access should be limited to what is necessary.

items.q: Can a student retake the assessment?

a.text: Yes, when there is a clear purpose. Record the version and date, and avoid treating small changes as major personality transformation.

items.q: Can Career Garage compare a student with national norms?

a.text: Not until a representative norming study has been completed for the relevant age and language group.

items.q: Can the English version simply be translated into Hindi?

a.text: No. It requires adaptation, cognitive interviewing and validation to show that meaning and scoring remain comparable.

items.q: Is Career Garage using the official BFI or NEO?

a.text: No. Version 1 is an original Career Garage instrument aligned with the broad Big Five framework.

items.q: When should a counsellor refer for additional support?

a.text: When a learner reports persistent distress, impairment, risk or a need beyond career guidance. The personality score itself is not the referral diagnosis.

sections.title: What is a type-preference framework?
sections.lead: A type language describes recurring orientations; good assessment practice still preserves the continuous evidence underneath.

blocks.text: Carl Jung's Psychological Types, first published in 1921, described introverted and extraverted attitudes and four orienting functions: sensation, intuition, thinking and feeling. items.q: Is this the official MBTI® assessment?

a.text: No. It is an original Career Garage instrument informed by broad preference-pair concepts. It must not be sold or described as an official MBTI assessment.

items.q: Why does the prompt mention Big Five?

a.text: The Big Five is a separate trait framework. This handbook includes a comparison because Career Garage may use both instruments, but their scores are not interchangeable.

items.q: Is one pole better than the other?

a.text: No. Every pole can support strengths and create trade-offs depending on the situation.

items.q: Does E mean good communication?

a.text: No. E concerns a reported preference for outward engagement. Communication is a learnable skill available at every score.

items.q: Does T mean logical and F mean emotional?

a.text: No. Both can reason and care. The pair concerns which decision criteria a learner tends to foreground.

items.q: Does J mean judgemental?

a.text: No. Planned Closure concerns structure and completion, not judging other people.

items.q: Why are there no reverse-scored items?

a.text: Version 1 measures each opposite pole with its own positive statements. This improves readability but creates acquiescence risk that must be tested.

items.q: Why use 64 questions?

a.text: Eight items per pole provide balanced coverage across eight poles while remaining practical for a pilot. Evidence, not item count alone, determines quality.

items.q: Can the system always produce one of 16 codes?

a.text: It can mechanically do so, but Career Garage should use X for pairs with very small differences or weak response quality.

items.q: Can a learner's code change?

a.text: Yes. Small differences, development, roles, language and context can change a code position. The underlying scores and examples matter more.

items.q: Can the result choose a career?

a.text: No. It can suggest environment questions. Career decisions require interests, aptitude, values, qualifications, opportunity and lived evidence.

items.q: Should all 13 assessments be taken together?

a.text: No. Use separate sessions or a carefully designed pathway to prevent fatigue and preserve informed consent.

items.q: Can teachers see raw answers?

a.text: Only if the published privacy, consent and role-access model authorises it. Default access should be limited to what is necessary.

items.q: When should a counsellor refer for support?

a.text: When a learner reports persistent distress, impairment, risk or a need beyond career guidance. A preference score is not a referral diagnosis.

sections.title: Executive overview
sections.lead: Career Garage uses motivation patterns as a reflection language, not as a permanent identity system.

blocks.alt: Career Garage Nine Motivation Pattern Map

blocks.text: Figure 1. Original Career Garage Nine Motivation Pattern Map. The map deliberately has no wings or directional arrows because those features are not scored in Version 1.

Two learners can display the same behaviour for different reasons. One may lead a project to achieve a visible target; another may lead to protect a group; another may lead because standards are slipping. Behaviour matters, but motive, attention and context help explain what sustains it.

sections.title: What is an Enneagram-inspired framework?
sections.lead: A nine-pattern language for exploring recurring motivations, attention habits and coping strategies.

blocks.text: The modern Enneagram of personality is a nine-type typology. Contemporary schools commonly describe one dominant type and may add wings, centres, levels and directional movements. The personality system is a modern twentieth-century synthesis rather than an unchanged ancient psychological test; even the Enneagram Institute's history places the type system's development in the 1960s around Oscar Ichazo's teaching, with later contributions from Claudio Naranjo and others.

items.q: Is this an official Enneagram test?

a.text: No. It is an original Career Garage instrument inspired by the broad idea of nine motivation patterns. It is not RHETI and is not affiliated with the Enneagram Institute or another school.

items.q: Why does this handbook discuss Big Five?

a.text: Career Garage includes both programs. Big Five is a separate continuous trait framework; this handbook explains how the two can complement each other without converting scores.

items.q: Why not assign one type?

a.text: The evidence does not justify treating nine types as fixed categories, especially for young learners. All nine continuous scores preserve more information and reduce labelling.

items.q: Why report the top three?

a.text: The top three organise reflection while acknowledging that several motives can be active. They are discussion priorities, not a new three-type identity.

items.q: Why are there no wings or arrows?

a.text: Research support for secondary features is limited, and those features are unnecessary for Version 1 career reflection.

items.q: Are high scores good?

a.text: No pattern is automatically good or bad. Every theme can contribute when flexible and create trade-offs when overused.

items.q: Can a low score improve?

a.text: Scores are not ability limits. A learner can practise behaviours associated with any pattern, whether or not the motive is strongly endorsed.

items.q: Can results change?

a.text: Yes. Context, development, language, current roles, item understanding and ordinary measurement error can affect scores.

items.q: Why use reverse-scored items?

a.text: They can reduce automatic agreement, but they can also confuse respondents. Career Garage must test their comprehension and method effects.

items.q: Are 72 questions enough?

a.text: The architecture gives eight items per pattern, but adequacy depends on content coverage and empirical evidence, not count alone.

items.q: Can the test choose a school stream or career?

a.text: No. It can suggest questions about motivating environments. Interests, aptitude, values, readiness, qualifications and experience are also required.

items.q: Can schools compare classrooms?

a.text: Only after fairness, aggregation, privacy and interpretation rules are established. Individual scores should not be used to label or rank classes.

items.q: Can parents see every answer?

a.text: Access follows the published age, consent and role model. The learner's dignity, privacy and safety remain central.

items.q: Can employers use the profile?

a.text: Career Garage should prohibit use for hiring, screening, promotion or exclusion.

items.q: Can AI write the report?

a.text: AI may personalise approved developmental language after deterministic scoring. It must not invent scores, cut-offs, diagnoses or career certainty.

items.q: When is counsellor review essential?

a.text: When scores conflict with experience, response-quality flags appear, distress is present or an important education or career decision is being considered.

sections.title: Overview
sections.lead: Four continuous work-style signals organised by pace and attention, with the complete profile preserved.

blocks.alt: Career Garage four work-style dimensions: Directing, Engaging, Stabilising and Systematic

blocks.text: Figure 1. Original Career Garage organising map. The two lenses are discussion aids, not separately scored axes.

The Career Garage model describes four ways a learner may approach shared work. Directing adds pace and ownership; Engaging adds energy and participation; Stabilising adds patience and continuity; Systematic adds evidence and standards. A learner has a score on every dimension and can use any behaviour deliberately.

sections.title: What is a work-style assessment?
sections.lead: It measures self-reported behavioural tendencies in defined work and learning contexts.

blocks.text: A work style is a recurring approach to tasks, communication, coordination, decisions and standards. The Career Garage assessment asks how often a learner recognises four broad approaches in usual situations and when demands increase. It does not observe the learner directly and cannot determine why a behaviour occurs.

sections.title: Historical roots and the modern landscape
sections.lead: Marston proposed four emotional-behaviour patterns; modern DISC assessments were developed later by different publishers.

blocks.text: William Moulton Marston's 1928 book Emotions of Normal People described Dominance, Inducement, Submission and Compliance as patterns of emotional expression in relation to a person's perception of the environment. Marston did not create the modern commercial questionnaires now sold under DISC-related names. Later developers translated, changed and commercialised the broad four-quadrant idea in different ways.

Each scale includes three core direct behaviours in general form, the same behaviours anchored in study/project/work, and the same behaviours under demand. items.q: Is this an official DiSC assessment?

a.text: No. It is an original Career Garage instrument with new scale names, items, scoring, figures and reports. It is not authorised or licensed by Wiley or another publisher.

items.q: Why not call learners D, I, S or C types?

a.text: A type label hides the complete profile and implies more certainty than Version 1 evidence supports. Career Garage reports four continuous scores.

items.q: Are high scores good?

a.text: No. High means the behaviour was endorsed more often, not that it is skilled, ethical or appropriate in every situation.

items.q: Can a learner have two or more high scores?

a.text: Yes. Several approaches can be strongly expressed. Discuss how they combine and which situations call for each.

items.q: Can results change?

a.text: Yes. Context, development, role, safety, language, current demands and ordinary measurement variation can affect results.

items.q: Does Directing mean leadership potential?

a.text: No. Leadership requires judgement, ethics, learning, communication and observed responsibility. No single style establishes potential.

items.q: Does Systematic mean intelligence?

a.text: No. It reflects reported evidence and standards behaviour, not cognitive ability.

items.q: Why are there reverse items?

a.text: They reduce simple agreement patterns but may create confusion. Career Garage must test comprehension and wording effects.

items.q: Can schools use the result to form teams?

a.text: Not as a sorting rule. Use voluntary discussion, observed skill, availability and development goals.

items.q: Can AI write the report?

a.text: AI may explain approved score-grounded content. Scoring remains deterministic and important guidance requires qualified human review.

sections.title: Overview
sections.lead: RIASEC organises career interests into six connected themes while preserving the learner's complete profile.

blocks.text: Figure 1. Original Career Garage representation of the six-theme interest map.

Holland's theory proposes that people and work environments can be described using six broad themes: Realistic, Investigative, Artistic, Social, Enterprising and Conventional. Career Garage turns those themes into six continuous interest scales. The result supports exploration of tasks, learning routes and work settings; it is not a label or a placement decision.

sections.title: What are vocational interests?
sections.lead: Interests concern attraction and engagement; they are distinct from ability, values and personality.

blocks.text: A vocational interest is a recurring preference for certain activities, subjects, problems or work environments. A learner may enjoy an activity before becoming skilled at it, or become skilled at a necessary activity without finding it energising. Interests are therefore useful for choosing what to explore and practise, but they cannot establish competence.

sections.title: Holland's RIASEC theory
sections.lead: A person-environment framework for understanding interests and occupational settings.

blocks.text: John L. Holland developed a theory of vocational personalities and work environments in which both people and environments can be represented using the same six themes. A person's pattern summarises preferred activities and settings. An environment's pattern summarises the activities, demands and rewards that are prominent there. Career development involves exploring whether a learner and an environment can support one another, not locating a single perfect occupation.

Items 09 and 10 are reverse-scored in each theme. Reverse wording is intended to reduce simple agreement patterns, but it can also create comprehension and method effects; those effects must be studied, especially across age and language groups.
Content standard

Each scale should cover several activities and contexts rather than repeat one stereotyped image. For example, Realistic items should not be limited to heavy tools, Social items should not be feminised, Enterprising items should not equate influence with wealth, and Conventional items should not imply low creativity or status.

items.q: Is RIASEC a personality test?

a.text: No. It measures self-reported attraction to career activities and environments. It should not be converted into a personality or ability label.

items.q: What does a three-letter code mean?

a.text: It summarises the three highest current interest scores. The full six-score profile, ties, context and uncertainty remain important.

items.q: Is a high score good?

a.text: No theme is better than another. A high score means stronger reported attraction in this item set, not greater talent, maturity or career value.

items.q: Can a learner have all high or all similar scores?

a.text: Yes. Broad exposure, broad attraction, central responding or item limitations can produce a flatter profile. Use examples and experiments rather than forcing differentiation.

items.q: Can interests change?

a.text: Yes. Interests can develop through exposure, learning, opportunity, identity and changing roles. Reports should include administration date, context and version.

items.q: Does an opposite-theme combination make the profile invalid?

a.text: No. R-S, I-E or A-C combinations may reflect varied tasks or contexts. Explore how both interests appear.

items.q: Can RIASEC select a school stream or degree?

a.text: Not by itself. Use subject preparation, aptitude, values, access, course requirements and experience alongside interests.

items.q: Why are there reverse items?

a.text: They reduce simple agreement patterns, but may also confuse respondents. Career Garage must test comprehension and method effects.

items.q: Is the Career Garage tool the O*NET Interest Profiler?

a.text: No. Career Garage uses an original item bank, scoring policy and report. It must not imply equivalence or affiliation.

items.q: Can AI make career recommendations?

a.text: AI may explain approved score-grounded hypotheses and actions. Deterministic scoring and qualified human review remain required for important decisions.

Career Garage treats emotions as information that can influence attention, judgement, action and relationships. The model asks what a learner usually notices and does with that information. The result is developmental: it should lead to a question, an observable practice and new evidence.

sections.title: What is emotional intelligence?
sections.lead: A broad label for reasoning about emotions, emotional self-perceptions and practical competencies.

blocks.text: Salovey and Mayer's early work described emotional intelligence as using information from one's own and others' emotions to guide thinking and action. Later ability models organised EI around perceiving, using, understanding and managing emotion. Other researchers developed trait models focused on emotional self-perceptions, while mixed models combined emotional skills with motives, dispositions and social competencies.

a.text: No. Version 1 reports five indices and does not publish a global EQ, percentile or emotional age.

items.q: Are high scores good?

a.text: High means the behaviour was endorsed more often. It does not prove effectiveness, boundaries, ethics or skill.

items.q: Can results change?

a.text: Yes. Development, language, context, safety, current demands, self-understanding and measurement variation can affect results.

items.q: Does high Empathy mean someone is kind?

a.text: No. The scale reflects reported perspective and cue-related behaviour, not moral character.

items.q: Does Self-Regulation mean staying calm?

a.text: No. Regulation can include healthy expression, boundaries, pausing, problem solving, rest or help-seeking.

items.q: Why is Internal Motivation included?

a.text: Career Garage uses a mixed competency framework. Motivation supports purposeful emotional action but is not a pure emotional ability.

items.q: Can the tool identify mental-health problems?

a.text: No. It must not diagnose or screen mental illness. Use safeguarding and qualified referral when a real concern arises.

items.q: Can schools use the profile for teams or leadership selection?

a.text: No. Use voluntary development conversations and independent evidence of skill, responsibility and readiness.

items.q: Can AI write the report?

a.text: AI may simplify approved score-grounded content. Scoring remains deterministic and important guidance requires qualified human review.

sections.title: What is career readiness?
sections.lead: Preparedness to explore, decide, demonstrate, pursue and adapt across education and work transitions.

blocks.text: Career readiness combines career-management knowledge, transferable behaviours, opportunity preparation and the capacity to turn goals into action. For Career Garage, readiness is developmental and contextual: it can grow through information, experience, feedback and structured practice, while access barriers remain separate from personal potential.

items.q: Can learners use AI for applications?

sections.title: Overview
sections.lead: Six current work priorities kept visible as a complete decision profile.

blocks.text: Career Garage treats the result as a priority profile, not a ladder. A higher score means a work condition was rated as more important after keying. It does not make the value more worthy or prove that an occupation will provide it. The useful question is whether credible evidence shows that a real opportunity can supply the learner's important conditions.

sections.title: What are work values?
sections.lead: Desired rewards, conditions and consequences that make work worth choosing or sustaining.

blocks.text: Work values describe what a person wants work to provide or make possible. They may concern challenge, independence, stability, contribution, relationships, learning, recognition, income, conditions or other rewards. Values are different from whether a learner enjoys an activity, can perform it or already has access to it.

items.q: Is one work value better than another?

a.text: No. Scores indicate current importance, not maturity, goodness, intelligence or employability.

items.q: Does the highest value choose the learner's career?

a.text: No. It creates evidence questions. Interests, capability, constraints and experience remain essential.

items.q: Is Security the same as fear of risk?

a.text: No. It concerns desired predictability and continuity; its meaning must be discussed in context.

items.q: Does Autonomy mean working alone?

a.text: No. It concerns meaningful choice and judgement within accountability, and can exist in collaborative teams.

items.q: Does Service and Impact require nonprofit work?

a.text: No. Positive contribution can appear in public, private, nonprofit, cooperative or entrepreneurial settings.

items.q: Can all six values be high?

a.text: Yes. Use relative priorities and explicit trade-offs; also review whether the learner answered ideally or without enough exposure.

items.q: Can results change?

a.text: Yes. Experience, life stage, responsibilities, scarcity, culture, opportunity and self-knowledge can shift priorities.

items.q: Will learners receive a match percentage?

a.text: No. Version 1 does not publish an overall fit score or automatic career match.

items.q: Can schools use the profile for stream allocation?

a.text: No. Use voluntary developmental guidance and multiple independent evidence sources.

items.q: Can employers use CG-WV for hiring?

a.text: No. The instrument is not designed or validated for selection.

items.q: Is CG-WV the MIQ or O*NET Work Importance Locator?

a.text: No. It is a separate original Career Garage instrument and its scores are not interchangeable.

sections.title: Overview

blocks.text: CG-LP describes methods a learner currently finds useful or appealing. A score becomes valuable only when translated into a strategy, tested on a real learning goal and compared with evidence of understanding, retention and transfer.

sections.title: What are learning preferences?
sections.lead: Self-reported tendencies toward particular ways of organising and engaging with learning.

blocks.text: A learning preference is a learner's current inclination toward certain study activities, representations or working conditions. Preferences can affect engagement, confidence and willingness to begin, but they do not by themselves establish which method produces the best learning outcome.

items.q: Is a learner's highest score their learning style?

a.text: No. It is a current self-reported preference, not a fixed type or prescription.

items.q: Should teachers match every lesson to the highest score?

a.text: No. Use task-appropriate, accessible instruction and multiple meaningful ways to engage and practise.

items.q: Can preferences be real even if matching is unsupported?

a.text: Yes. Preferences can influence engagement and choice, but effectiveness must be tested with outcomes.

items.q: Does a lower Visual score mean weak visual ability?

a.text: No. CG-LP does not measure aptitude, perception or memory ability.

items.q: Can all four preferences be high?

a.text: Yes. This may indicate broad flexibility, idealised responding or strong endorsement; use examples and outcomes.

items.q: Can scores change?

a.text: Yes. Task, experience, language, access, motivation and strategy training can shift responses.

items.q: Does Active Experience mean movement?

a.text: Not necessarily. It means purposeful application or rehearsal linked to the learning goal.

items.q: Can schools group students by CG-LP profile?

a.text: No. Grouping or restricting instruction from preference scores is a prohibited Version 1 use.

items.q: Can CG-LP diagnose dyslexia, ADHD or a learning disability?

a.text: No. It is not a diagnostic or screening instrument.

items.q: Does the profile choose a course or career?

a.text: No. It can inform learning plans inside broader career guidance, but not suitability.

sections.title: What is digital skills readiness?

blocks.text: Digital competence includes the knowledge, skills and attitudes needed to engage confidently, critically, safely and responsibly with digital technologies. Readiness is narrower: it asks how prepared a learner currently feels to perform essential behaviours and where practical evidence or support should be added.

sections.title: What is an entrepreneurial mindset?
sections.lead: A developable pattern of attention, judgement and action—not a job title.

blocks.text: Entrepreneurship can be understood as creating value by acting on ideas and opportunities while mobilising resources under uncertainty. Value may be financial, social, cultural or organisational. This makes entrepreneurial competence relevant not only to founders, but also to students, employees, freelancers, family enterprises and community innovators.

items.q: Does a high score mean I should start a business?

items.q: Does CG-EM predict success?

items.q: Is there a best profile?

a.text: No. Different tasks require different balances, teams and contextual resources.

items.q: Is Risk Judgement the same as risk tolerance?

a.text: No. CG-EM emphasises considered, testable decisions and safeguards, not appetite for danger.

items.q: Does Resilience mean never giving up?

a.text: No. Responsible resilience includes recovery, support, pivoting and stopping when evidence or wellbeing requires it.

items.q: Can scores change?

sections.title: Cognitive Aptitude Profile
sections.lead: See how you approach unfamiliar problems.

blocks.text: The Career Garage Cognitive Aptitude Profile uses original objective questions to sample reasoning across several domains. The report shows current performance, strategy patterns and practice priorities - not a fixed measure of intelligence or potential.

blocks.alt: Cognitive Aptitude Profile: six reasoning domains

sections.title: What this assessment helps you understand

blocks.text: Aptitude performance reflects both reasoning and conditions such as familiarity, language, education, disability, fatigue and test anxiety. Career Garage therefore reports domain evidence and item explanations rather than reducing a learner to one global label.

Objective items have one defensible answer, mapped skill and rationale. For operational use, Career Garage should maintain secure forms, accommodations, calibrated timing, item analysis and version-controlled norms based on relevant samples.
What it measures

rows: Understanding relationships, arguments and meaning in written information.
Interpreting quantities, ratios, patterns and numerical evidence.
Drawing valid conclusions from rules, conditions and sequences.
Recognising transformations, structures and visual relationships.
Reading tables, charts and multi-step quantitative information.
Maintaining accuracy, choosing strategies and checking work.

items: Select an age-appropriate form and any approved accessibility accommodations.
Complete original verbal, numerical, logical, spatial and data tasks.

Domain results are interpreted only against documented scoring rules or validated norms.
Worked explanations reveal strategy errors and practice opportunities.
Counsellors combine performance with interests, education and real achievements.

blocks.text: What your report includes

items: Separate performance indicators for every reasoning domain
Accuracy and timing information kept conceptually distinct
Worked answers and common error patterns
Practice priorities and sample skill-building activities
Career and course demands to investigate
Accommodation and interpretation notes for professionals

blocks.text: Career connection

Aptitude can inform preparation, but it should not close doors. Many capabilities grow through teaching and practice, and real careers rely on knowledge, motivation, collaboration, creativity and opportunity as well as reasoning tests.

blocks.label: INTERPRETATION BOUNDARY
blocks.text: No IQ, percentile, ability label or high-stakes decision until timing, reliability, validity, forms and norms are supported.

items.q: Is this an IQ test?

a.text: No. It samples defined reasoning domains for career-development purposes and does not claim to measure global intelligence.

items.q: Can I improve my performance?

a.text: Strategy, familiarity, knowledge and practice can improve performance. Large decisions should consider broader evidence.

items.q: What happens if I skip a question?

a.text: Unanswered objective items remain missing, not automatically incorrect, unless a timed-administration policy was pre-specified, communicated and supported by validation. Version 1 totals require all 60 attempted.

items.q: Will I get an IQ score or percentile?

a.text: No IQ, percentile, ability label or high-stakes decision until timing, reliability, validity, forms and norms are supported.

items.q: Can this score be used for admission or selection?

a.text: Aptitude testing can become high stakes. Use age-appropriate secure forms, trained oversight, fair accommodations, relevant norms and documented validity before any selection use. Never interpret one score in isolation.
